definition: A roof inspection is a systematic evaluation of a roof's covering, flashing, drainage, ventilation, sealants, and deck that rates each component by condition and documents damage, wear, and active-leak indications before water reaches the interior.

costRanges.item: Drone roof inspection (steep or large roof surveyed from the air)
Infrared roof inspection (highest-cost method; locates trapped moisture invisible to the eye)

costRanges.range: $75–$600 for most inspections (this is a per-method price band, NOT a single whole-job total; cost is set by roof size, slope, accessibility, and inspection method). Newark Quality Roofing provides a free roof inspection.
costRanges.source: HomeAdvisor inspection-cost data (gold pricing.range); free-inspection offer per Newark Quality Roofing gold whyChooseUs/FAQ

signs: A roof age past 10 years without a documented inspection in the prior 2 years marks the point for a professional roof inspection, because most asphalt roofs serve roughly 20 years — per the NRCA (which recommends an inspection at least twice per year).

A major weather event — severe wind at 58 mph or above, or hail ¾ inch or larger — triggers a roof inspection even with no visible damage from the ground; the 58 mph wind and ¾ inch hail severe-weather thresholds are set by NOAA, and the NRCA recommends an added inspection after any major storm.

A home purchase or sale calls for an independent roof inspection that reports roof-covering condition and active-leak indications, per the InterNACHI roof inspection standard of practice, before the roof becomes a transaction negotiation point.

Granule loss with sandy grit in gutters signals shingles nearing end of life; granule loss exceeding 30% of the surface is the common rule-of-thumb for beyond repair, and 50% loss cuts remaining life by up to 70% — per GAF.

Brown or yellow ceiling and wall stains that spread after rainfall indicate an active roof leak or trapped attic moisture, the condition a pre-leak moisture inspection detects before the stain appears — per GAF and This Old House inspection guidance.

An insurance or manufacturer-warranty inspection requirement prompts a documented roof inspection, because many commercial policies and manufacturer warranties condition coverage on annual professional inspections — per the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I).

selectionCriteria.criterion: Active New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor (HIC) registration
selectionCriteria.detail: Verify the contractor holds an active NJ HIC registration (N.J.S.A. 56:8-136). The 13VH registration number must appear on the contract and in advertising (N.J.S.A. 56:8-144). This is a registration, NOT a license — New Jersey issues no roofing license. NQR is a registered NJ HIC.
selectionCriteria.source: N.J.S.A. 56:8-136; N.J.S.A. 56:8-144 (NJ Contractors Registration Act); NJ Division of Consumer Affairs

selectionCriteria.criterion: Commercial general liability insurance, minimum $500,000 per occurrence
selectionCriteria.detail: A registered NJ HIC must carry commercial general liability insurance of at least $500,000 per occurrence (N.J.S.A. 56:8-142). Confirm coverage by requesting a Certificate of Insurance issued directly by the contractor's insurance carrier.

New Jersey requires a written, signed contract for any home-improvement work priced over $500 (N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2). The contract must state the work scope, total price, and the contractor's 13VH registration number.
selectionCriteria.source: N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2 (NJ Consumer Fraud Act / Home Improvement Practices regulations)

selectionCriteria.detail: A trustworthy inspector delivers a written, itemized estimate of any recommended work rather than a verbal figure, so the homeowner can compare scope and price.

Choose a contractor whose inspection produces a written condition report — each component rated by urgency, photographs keyed to a roof diagram, roof-covering type recorded, and active-leak indications reported — consistent with the InterNACHI roof inspection standard of practice. This is the documentation an insurance carrier or manufacturer-warranty program accepts (per the Insurance Information Institute).
selectionCriteria.source: InterNACHI roof inspection standard of practice; Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I)

selectionCriteria.criterion: Local references and established local presence
selectionCriteria.detail: Favor a contractor with verifiable local references and an established Essex County / New Jersey presence familiar with the area's freeze-thaw and storm seasons and with NJ permitting under N.J.A.C. 5:23.
selectionCriteria.source: Newark Quality Roofing gold (Local Essex County Roofers); N.J.A.C. 5:23 (NJ Uniform Construction Code)

technicalFacts.fact: The roofing industry estimates that roughly 90–95% of roof leaks originate at flashing and only 5–10% at the open shingle field, so a thorough inspection starts at the flashing details.
technicalFacts.source: Industry estimate attributed to the NRCA

technicalFacts.fact: The NRCA recommends a roof inspection at least twice per year — spring and fall — plus an additional inspection after any major weather event.
Proper maintenance on the twice-per-year inspection cadence extends asphalt-shingle service life by roughly 25–30%.

Sealing the roof deck cuts water intrusion into the home by up to 95% versus an unsealed deck, so a pre-leak moisture inspection (moisture meters on deck and framing, infrared imaging) can find a failing detail while a repair stays minor.
technicalFacts.source: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)

technicalFacts.fact: Attic ventilation should provide 1 square foot of net-free vent area per 150 square feet of attic floor, balanced about 50% intake and 50% exhaust; balanced ventilation extends roof service life by up to 25%.
technicalFacts.source: NRCA and ARMA (1:150 ratio); NRCA (service-life extension)

technicalFacts.fact: A flat (low-slope) roof needs at least ¼ inch per foot of positive slope to drain; ponding water remaining more than 48 hours counts as a defect that accelerates membrane deterioration.

Wind and hail rank as the largest homeowners-insurance claim type at 2.8% of insured homes per year (1 in 36), so a documented storm inspection with timestamped photographs supports a claim for damage invisible from the ground.
NOAA sets the severe-weather thresholds of 58 mph wind and ¾ inch hail — the levels at which a post-storm roof inspection is warranted even with no ground-visible damage.
The InterNACHI roof inspection standard of practice directs an inspector to describe the roof-covering type and report observed indications of active roof leaks.

Repair/replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling counts as ordinary maintenance — no construction permit, inspection, or notice required — so an inspection report documents condition rather than triggering a permit.

On a commercial building, repairing more than 25% of the total roof area within a 12-month period requires a permit, so an inspection report should size the affected area before a repair scope sets the permit path.

Membrane life expectancy on commercial low-slope roofs: EPDM 15–25 years, TPO 7–20 years, modified bitumen 20 years; EPDM fails most often at the seams and TPO at the welded seams — the detail a commercial inspection targets.

Repair-vs-replace thresholds: repair when localized damage is under 25–30% of the roof area; replace when damage exceeds 25–30% of the area or one repair approaches 50% of replacement cost (contractor-consensus thresholds); granule loss above 30% of the surface marks shingles as beyond repair (per GAF).
technicalFacts.source: Contractor-consensus thresholds (25–30% area, 50% cost rule); GAF (granule-loss rule)

sources: InterNACHI (roof inspection standard of practice; life-expectancy chart)
Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)

defabToKill.issue: Vague invented authority: 'New Jersey building science professionals recommend annual inspections for roofs over ten years old and biennial inspections for newer roofs.' No such NJ-specific source exists in the gold.
defabToKill.fix: Use the grounded NRCA cadence: inspect at least twice per year, spring and fall, plus an additional inspection after any major weather event (NRCA). Tie the 'past 2 years / over 10 years' framing to the gold sign and the ~20-year asphalt service life (NRCA), not to unnamed 'building science professionals.'

defabToKill.issue: Wrong storm threshold: 'winds exceeding 50 mph, hail of any size.' Gold/NOAA severe-weather thresholds are 58 mph wind and ¾ inch hail.
defabToKill.fix: State the NOAA thresholds: severe wind at 58 mph or above, or hail ¾ inch or larger, triggers an inspection (NOAA); the NRCA recommends an added inspection after any major storm.

defabToKill.issue: Invented insurance-deadline claim: 'Insurance companies in New Jersey typically allow one year from a storm event to file a damage claim.' No source; claim windows vary by policy.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the one-year deadline. Ground the storm-inspection value in the III figure: wind and hail are the largest homeowners-claim type at 2.8%/year (1 in 36), and a documented inspection with timestamped photos records damage invisible from the ground (Insurance Information Institute).

defabToKill.issue: Fabricated operational stat / self-claim: 'We schedule the majority of our Essex County inspections between mid-March and late April.' Invented internal scheduling data.
defabToKill.fix: Remove the invented scheduling claim. Keep the spring-window rationale grounded in NRCA spring/fall cadence and freeze-thaw stress, framed qualitatively (no internal percentages).

defabToKill.issue: Off-scope ventilation/energy-bill framing presented as roof-inspection 'subtle signs' (energy spikes, window condensation, musty odors framed as roof ventilation problems) without sourcing.
defabToKill.fix: If ventilation is mentioned, ground it in the NRCA/ARMA 1:150 net-free-vent ratio (50% intake / 50% exhaust) and the up-to-25% service-life extension from balanced ventilation (NRCA). Keep granule loss / ceiling stains as the primary grounded signs (GAF; GAF + This Old House).

defabToKill.issue: Fabricated repair-cost ROI statistics: 'average Essex County roof repair costs $750 to $2,500 ... but $5,000 to $15,000 when allowed to progress', '$250 annual inspection ... save ten to twenty times its cost', '$5,000 to $6,000 in cumulative inspection costs.' No sourced repair-cost data in the inspection gold.
defabToKill.fix: Remove the invented repair-cost ranges and 10x–20x ROI math. Ground the value of inspection in sourced facts only: proper maintenance extends asphalt-shingle life ~25–30% (ARMA); sealing the deck cuts water intrusion up to 95% (IBHS); early detection keeps a repair minor. No dollar ROI figures.

defabToKill.fix: Drop the premium-discount claim. The grounded insurance angle is that many commercial policies and manufacturer warranties condition coverage on annual professional inspections (Insurance Information Institute), and a documented inspection supports a storm-damage claim.

defabToKill.fix: Replace with the gold offer: Newark Quality Roofing provides a free roof inspection. Use HomeAdvisor figures only for the market-pricing context, not as NQR's price.
